strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful, underexplored problem: separately detecting cast and attached shadows. The curated annotations could support research beyond conventional binary shadow detection, and the source datasets and component methods are appropriately acknowledged.

The reported attached-shadow improvement is substantial: Table 2 reduces BER from the strongest retrained baseline’s 19.49 to 12.93, approximately 34%, while increasing attached-shadow F1 to 86.49. Full-shadow and cast-shadow F1 are also competitive.

Table 3 provides useful evidence for geometry guidance and iterative refinement. Adding normals reduces attached BER from 20.87 to 15.10, and the three-iteration model further reduces it to 12.92. These comparisons support the practical value of the proposed components.

The overall framework is understandable, and the paper candidly discusses inaccurate geometry, the single-directional-light assumption, missing instance associations, and the increased inference cost.
weaknesses: The light-estimation objective has a consequential mathematical ambiguity. Equation (1) defines the partial attached-shadow map using a hard binary threshold, but Equation (7) applies BCE to this map to train the light estimator. As written, the threshold provides no useful gradient to the predicted direction, and probability-space BCE on incorrect exact binary predictions is singular without numerical clipping. No differentiable relaxation or gradient estimator is specified. This also prevents segmentation gradients from traversing the stated feedback map and makes the reported benefit of Latt difficult to reconcile with the formulation.

The central claim that shadow and light estimation improve each other is only partially evaluated. The experiments report segmentation metrics, but no light-direction angular errors, per-iteration lighting accuracy, or quantitative quality of the geometry-derived masks. The calibrated WSRD subset could provide a particularly useful independent test. Segmentation gains alone do not establish that the inferred illumination becomes more physically accurate.

The heuristic lighting targets are insufficiently justified and specified. An object-to-shadow centroid displacement is not generally the image-plane projection of the illumination ray under perspective projection and arbitrary receiving geometry. The procedure also does not specify how the depth-derived component is scaled relative to image coordinates. Likewise, converting relative depth into camera-frame normals requires geometric assumptions that are not described. These issues matter because the resulting directions and normals provide the physical supervision underlying the method.

The benchmark needs stronger validation and documentation. Annotation is restricted to selected foreground objects, and attached-shadow evaluation is restricted to object regions, leaving erroneous attached predictions elsewhere unmeasured. The supplied manuscript lacks annotator agreement, detailed rules for ambiguous self-occlusion and shadow ownership, and scene-level split or duplicate-control information. The listed source counts also total 1,468 rather than the stated 1,458; this numerical discrepancy is minor by itself, but the annotation and split uncertainties materially affect confidence in the benchmark.

The comparisons do not fully isolate the distinctive contribution of physical feedback. Retrained baselines receive binary full-shadow supervision, whereas the proposed model receives category labels, normals, and lighting targets. The multiclass and non-iterative ablations help, but a matched generic recurrent refinement baseline would better separate physical reasoning from additional iterative computation. Evidence is also limited to the curated test set without uncertainty estimates or external validation. The claimed broad performance advantage should be qualified: full-shadow BER improves only from 6.51 to 6.50, and cast BER is worse than the strongest baseline.

strengths: The paper addresses a worthwhile, underexplored problem: separately detecting cast and attached shadows. The curated annotations could support research beyond conventional binary shadow detection. I assess the submission as Algorithms/General, while also crediting its dataset contribution.

Table 2 shows substantial attached-shadow gains: BER decreases from the best retrained baseline's 19.49 to 12.93, approximately a 34% relative reduction, and F1 increases from 82.69 to 86.49. These results support the practical value of incorporating geometry and distinguishing shadow types.

Table 3 provides useful component evidence. Attached-shadow BER improves from 20.87 without normals to 15.10 with the non-iterative configuration and 12.92 with three iterations. The qualitative comparisons also illustrate improved attached-shadow localization.

The manuscript clearly motivates the geometry–illumination relationship, attributes its source datasets and pretrained components, and acknowledges meaningful limitations concerning inaccurate normals, multiple lights, and missing instance associations.
weaknesses: The central light-consistency objective is not technically reproducible as written. Equation (1) produces a hard binary map through a sign threshold, and Equation (7) applies weighted BCE directly to that map. The threshold supplies no useful ordinary gradient to the predicted light direction; probability-space BCE additionally encounters singularities at incorrect binary predictions unless numerically clamped. No differentiable relaxation or gradient estimator is specified. Although the direction-regression loss could still train the estimator, the claimed optimization role of the attached-shadow consistency loss, and its reported ablation benefit, require an explanation of the actual implementation.

The claim that shadow detection and light estimation mutually improve is only evaluated on the shadow side. There are no angular-error measurements, per-iteration lighting results, or independent checks on the calibrated WSRD subset. For SOBA/CUHK, combining image-plane centroid displacement with relative depth does not establish a calibrated 3D light direction: the relative scaling of these components, perspective projection, and receiving-surface geometry matter. Likewise, the conversion from relative depth to physically meaningful normals is insufficiently specified. Consequently, the results demonstrate useful geometric features more convincingly than accurate illumination recovery.

The experiments only partially isolate the proposed physical feedback mechanism. Retrained external baselines receive full-shadow supervision, whereas the proposed model additionally receives subclass supervision, normals, and lighting targets. The no-normal and non-iterative ablations help address this, but there is no comparable recurrent segmentation control without physical feedback, or fixed/shuffled-light control, to distinguish the value of the specific lighting mechanism from additional computation and auxiliary supervision. This matters because three iterations roughly triple processing time.

The dataset contribution needs stronger validation. The supplied manuscript does not establish annotation agreement, adjudication criteria for ambiguous attached shadows, or how scene/object overlap is prevented across the split. Evaluation is restricted to selected foreground objects for attached shadows, so it does not quantitatively substantiate the broader scene-wide labeling claims illustrated in Figure 6. Source-specific results or an independent evaluation would help establish generalization beyond the curated 292-image test set. There is also a minor count inconsistency: the stated source totals, 220 + 710 + 538, sum to 1,468 rather than 1,458.

Some performance claims exceed the evidence. Full-shadow BER is essentially tied with retrained SILT (6.50 versus 6.51), while cast BER is worse (5.04 versus 4.52). Iteration and loss ablations also show tradeoffs across metrics rather than uniformly improving performance. These observations do not negate the strong attached-shadow result, but the absence of variability estimates limits conclusions about small differences. Overall, the promising task and segmentation gains are outweighed by unresolved concerns about the central training formulation and the evidence for physically meaningful mutual refinement.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful, underexplored problem: separately detecting cast and attached shadows. The proposed annotations could support research beyond conventional binary shadow detection.

The combination of surface orientation, estimated illumination, and iterative segmentation is well motivated. The paper appropriately acknowledges earlier joint shadow–illumination reasoning and limitations involving geometry errors and multiple light sources.

Table 2 reports substantial attached-shadow improvements: BER decreases from the strongest retrained baseline's 19.49 to 12.93, approximately 34%, while F1 increases from 82.69 to 86.49. Full-shadow and cast-shadow F1 also improve.

Table 3 provides useful component ablations. Normal guidance and iterative feedback both improve attached-shadow detection, with feedback reducing BER from 15.10 to 12.92. Qualitative examples support the segmentation benefits.
weaknesses: The central training formulation has an unresolved differentiability problem. Equation (1) defines a hard binary threshold, but Equation (7) applies BCE directly to that map to train the light estimator. This threshold supplies no useful gradient with respect to light direction, and BCE on binary probabilities is singular for mismatches without numerical clipping. A differentiable surrogate or gradient estimator is not specified. This materially affects reproducibility and interpretation of the reported loss ablation.

The claim that iterative reasoning improves light estimation is not quantitatively tested. No angular errors, lighting baselines, or per-iteration lighting measurements are reported, even for the WSRD subset described as having ground-truth directions. Segmentation improvements alone do not establish physically accurate illumination recovery.

The geometric supervision is insufficiently specified and validated. Combining image-plane centroid displacement with relative depth requires a defined coordinate conversion and relative scaling; depth ordering alone does not determine a 3D direction. Likewise, converting relative depth into camera-frame normals requires assumptions that are not given. These uncertainties directly affect the physical interpretation of the feedback map.

Baseline comparisons conflate geometry, supervision, and architecture: retrained competitors receive full-shadow labels, whereas the proposed model receives separate class labels and normals. The internal ablations partly address this, but a matched RGB-plus-normal, three-class detector and a comparable recurrent model without the physical map would better isolate the proposed mechanism.

The dataset contribution needs stronger documentation and validation. The supplied manuscript does not establish annotation agreement, scene-disjoint split construction, or generalization beyond the curated test set. Object-restricted attached-shadow evaluation also leaves whole-image separation insufficiently tested. Additionally, the listed source counts sum to 1,468 images rather than the stated 1,458; this is a minor correction, but the broader protocol omissions matter.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful, underexplored problem: explicitly separating cast and attached shadows. The 1,458-image dataset with separate annotations is a potentially valuable contribution alongside the algorithm.

The reciprocal use of geometry, lighting, and shadow predictions is well motivated. The manuscript appropriately attributes earlier joint shadow/illumination inference and clearly explains its iterative neural formulation.

Attached-shadow improvements are substantial: Table 2 reports BER of 12.93 versus 19.49 for the strongest fine-tuned baseline, with F1 increasing from 82.69 to 86.49 relative to the strongest baseline on that metric. Full-shadow performance remains competitive.

The experiments include useful component ablations, normal-augmented baselines in the supplement, inference timings, and calibrated-subset lighting evaluation. The non-iterative versus three-iteration comparison supports an additional benefit from feedback for attached-shadow detection.

The downstream removal study provides encouraging evidence of practical relevance, and the limitations discussion appropriately acknowledges dependence on estimated geometry and the single-directional-light assumption.
weaknesses: The central training objective is not technically specified in a reproducible, differentiable form. Equation (1) produces a hard binary mask, yet Equation (7) applies BCE to that mask to train the light estimator. The threshold has zero derivative almost everywhere, and mismatched binary probabilities give unbounded BCE without numerical clipping. No soft surrogate or gradient estimator is described. Thus, the claimed role and reported ablation effect of L_att cannot be explained by the stated equations. Gradient handling and loss accumulation across iterations also need clarification.

The physical geometry has unresolved coordinate and scale inconsistencies. Supplement Section 3.3 constructs normals with z=1 and defines positive z toward the camera, whereas lighting uses positive z inward. No conversion is documented before their dot product. Moreover, relative-depth gradients are treated as surface normals, and pixel centroid displacement is combined with relative-depth differences to construct a 3D light vector without specifying compatible scales or camera geometry. These approximations may provide useful learned cues, but the current account does not establish the claimed physical consistency.

The benchmark needs stronger independent annotation validation. SOBA attached masks are initialized using the same normal/light construction that motivates the proposed method, then manually corrected, but annotator agreement, correction criteria, and an independent audit are not reported. WSRD separates shadows by object-mask membership, which does not distinguish orientation-induced attached shadow from occlusion-induced self-shadow. These choices leave uncertainty about both annotation bias and the precise target concept. Scene/object grouping and duplicate handling in the train/test split are also unspecified.

The comparisons do not fully isolate the proposed lighting mechanism. Fine-tuned prior methods receive binary full-shadow supervision, while the proposed model receives subclass labels, geometry, and light supervision. The no-normal multiclass variant and normal-augmented binary baselines are useful, but a matched RGB-plus-normal multiclass detector without the light module, and a comparable generic recurrent refinement baseline, are missing. The evidence therefore supports the combined system more strongly than the necessity of physically structured feedback.

Validation beyond the curated benchmark remains limited. Cross-dataset results are qualitative, and lighting accuracy is measured on only 42 WSRD images from the described fixed acquisition setup, without a constant-direction baseline or angular errors. This provides limited evidence for lighting recovery under diverse illumination. The removal comparison also changes the refinement procedure as well as mask granularity; its 259 votes lack participant counts and uncertainty estimates. These experiments are promising demonstrations but do not yet substantiate broad generalization or isolate the downstream value of shadow-type separation.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful, underexplored distinction between cast and attached shadows. Separating these outputs could benefit scene understanding and shadow removal. I assess the submission as Algorithms/General, while also crediting its dataset contribution.

The 1,458-image dataset adds explicit cast/attached annotations to three attributed public sources. Excluding ambiguous, undefined regions from type-specific supervision and evaluation is a reasonable design choice, and the supplement explains the annotation workflow.

The reported attached-shadow improvement is substantial: Table 2 gives BER 12.93 versus 19.49 for the strongest fine-tuned baseline, with F1 increasing to 86.49. Full-shadow performance remains competitive, although cast BER is not best.

The experimental analysis includes geometry, iteration-count, and loss ablations; supplementary normal-augmented baselines; runtime measurements; and light-estimation evaluation. The non-iterative-to-three-iteration improvement in attached BER from 15.10 to 12.92 supports the usefulness of feedback. The limitations concerning estimated geometry and complex lighting are appropriately acknowledged.
weaknesses: The stated training objective has an unresolved differentiability problem. Equation (1) defines the partial attached-shadow map using a hard threshold, while Equation (7) applies weighted BCE to that map to train the light estimator. As written, thresholding supplies no useful gradient to the light direction; BCE on exact binary probabilities also requires handling mismatches at zero and one. No differentiable relaxation, surrogate gradient, or alternative optimization is specified. This is consequential because the paper attributes improvements to this loss and reports an ablation for it. The actual computational graph, gradient paths, and iteration-wise optimization need to be documented.

The physical geometry formulation is insufficiently consistent. Supplement Section 3.3 defines normals with positive z toward the camera, whereas the light vectors use positive z into the scene. Their dot product requires an explicit common-coordinate transformation, which is not described. Furthermore, normals formed from relative-depth gradients depend on depth scaling and projection assumptions, while the heuristic light vector combines image-plane centroid displacement with relative-depth difference without explaining compatible units. These may yield useful learned cues, but their interpretation as physically meaningful 3D lighting and surface orientation is not established.

The benchmark annotations are not fully independent of the proposed prior. Supplement Section 3.1 initializes SOBA attached masks using the same estimated normals and derived lighting that motivate the method, followed by manual correction. This does not establish invalidity, but creates a plausible annotation bias favoring geometry-consistent predictions. Independent annotation checks, inter-annotator agreement, and per-source results would help determine whether the gains reflect accurate shadow detection rather than agreement with the annotation initializer. The train/test split procedure and scene or object overlap controls are also unspecified.

The comparisons do not cleanly isolate the proposed lighting mechanism. Fine-tuned prior methods receive binary full-shadow supervision and are split using object masks, whereas the proposed model receives explicit type supervision, geometry, and auxiliary lighting targets. The multiclass and normal-augmented ablations partially address this, but a matched RGB-plus-normal multiclass detector without the light estimator, alongside a comparable recurrent-refinement baseline, would better separate the value of physical feedback from supervision, capacity, and repeated computation. The headline 33% gain should therefore be interpreted as a complete-system comparison.

Evidence for accurate physical light recovery and broad generalization remains limited. Light accuracy is measured only on 42 WSRD images from a fixed calibrated acquisition setup; a constant-direction baseline and angular errors are needed to establish how demanding this evaluation is. Cross-dataset results are qualitative, and temporal consistency is inferred from examples rather than measured. These results demonstrate feasibility but do not substantiate broad robustness claims.

The shadow-removal study is encouraging but confounded: the separate-mask condition also adds object-region refinement, so the preference cannot be attributed solely to distinguishing shadow types. The refinement procedure and participant count are not sufficiently specified, and uncertainty accounting for repeated participants and images is absent. The statement that shadow-free ground truth is unavailable also needs qualification because the WSRD subset is explicitly described as paired. Overall, the promising empirical gains do not yet outweigh the unresolved training and physical-model issues.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful, underexplored problem: explicitly separating cast and attached shadows. The combination of a dedicated dataset and a geometry-aware detector has potential value for scene understanding and shadow editing.

The reported attached-shadow improvement is substantial: BER decreases from 19.49 for the strongest retrained baseline to 12.93, approximately a 34% relative reduction, while attached F1 reaches 86.49. The qualitative comparisons also show improved separation.

The ablations support the usefulness of geometry and iterative feedback. Attached BER improves from 20.87 without normals to 15.10 with the non-iterative geometry-aware model, and to 12.92 with three iterations. The supplement additionally evaluates normal-augmented baselines and reports computational costs.

The 1,458-image dataset explicitly distinguishes cast, attached, and undefined shadows, with attribution to its source datasets. Excluding ambiguous regions from subtype supervision is a reasonable design choice.

The manuscript clearly motivates the approach, acknowledges relevant earlier joint shadow–illumination inference, and discusses dependence on normal quality and the single-directional-light assumption.
weaknesses: The training formulation has an unresolved technical inconsistency. Equation (1) defines the partial attached mask using a hard threshold, but Equation (7) applies BCE to that binary mask to supervise lighting. As written, the threshold supplies no useful gradient to the light estimator, and probability-form BCE is singular for incorrect exact-zero/one predictions. No differentiable relaxation or gradient estimator is specified. This directly affects reproducibility and interpretation of the reported L_att ablation.

The physical geometry is insufficiently justified. Supplement Section 3.3 constructs normals from relative-depth gradients with z fixed to 1, without specifying depth scaling or camera calibration. Section 3.5 combines image-plane centroid offsets and relative-depth differences into a purported 3D light vector, although these quantities have incompatible scales without additional assumptions. Moreover, normals use +z toward the camera while light directions use +z inward, with no coordinate conversion described. These issues affect the central normal–light dot product, rather than merely presentation.

The annotation process risks favoring the proposed prior: SOBA attached labels begin from light-and-normal-derived masks and are manually corrected. The manuscript provides correction examples but no independent annotation audit, agreement measurements, or annotation criteria for ambiguous shading and self-occlusion. Scene/object separation in the train/test split is also unspecified. Given that the principal quantitative evidence comes from this newly constructed benchmark, these omissions materially limit confidence in generalization.

The evidence does not fully isolate the benefit of physical iterative reasoning. The non-iterative and normal-augmented controls are useful, but a matched recurrent detector without the physical map would clarify whether gains come from the proposed feedback or additional computation. Lighting accuracy is evaluated only on 42 WSRD images from a fixed calibrated lighting setup, without a constant-direction baseline; this provides limited evidence for scene-dependent illumination recovery. Cross-dataset results are qualitative only.

The shadow-removal study is encouraging but confounded: the separate-mask condition also adds object-region refinement, so its 80.7% preference cannot be attributed solely to mask separation. The supplement reports 259 votes but omits participant count and uncertainty accounting for repeated participants/images. Overall, the promising empirical gains do not yet outweigh the unresolved training and geometry issues under an Algorithms/General assessment.
